## Query on the Single Order with Lazy Loading

If you want to issue a query on the single Order entity with lazy loading, you need to use the GetOrder method of the OrderEntities context object to return a single order. In this case, you cannot rely on the lazy loading because lazy loading requires the creation of a new context to automatically load the OrderDetails for the Order. The solution is to use the Include method that changes the default behavior and enables the return of the related entities. The following code shows an example of this approach:
```
using (var context = new OrderEntities())
{
    var order = context.Orders
                   .Include("OrderDetails")
                   .First(o => o.OrderID == orderId);
    //...
}
```
## Query on Orders with Eager Loading

If you want to load all the orders and the OrderDetails in a single query, you can use the Include method, working with eager loading to return a set of orders and the related OrderDetails :
```
using (var context = new OrderEntities())
{
    var orders = context.Orders.Include("OrderDetails").ToList();
    //...
}
```
## Use the Query Builder Methods

You can use the query builder methods—such as Where, OrderBy, and Select —to define a query that will be converted in the corresponding SQL statement. For example, you can issue a query to retrieve only the orders with an EmployeeID equal to 2 and TotalDue greater than 200 :
```
from o in context.Orders
where o.EmployeeID == 2 && o.TotalDue > 200
select new { o.OrderID, o.OrderDate, o.TotalDue };
```
You can use these methods to retrieve a related entity, such as retrieving the OrderDetails by defining a Select statement that returns an anonymous type for each order. For example, the following code sample defines a complex query that retrieves the orders with an EmployeeID equal to 2 and TotalDue greater than 200, and returns a new set of anonymous objects that contains the OrderID, OrderDate, and the related OrderDetails :
```
from o in context.Orders
where o.EmployeeID == 2 && o.TotalDue > 200
orderby o.TotalDue descending
select new
{
    o.OrderID,
    o.OrderDate,
    Details = o.OrderDetails.Select(d => new
    {
        d.ProductID,
        d.UnitPrice,
        d.Quantity,
        d.UnitPriceDiscount
    })
};
```
In this case, you can see that the Select method provides a way to project data into a structure that’s different from the default entity structure. This is useful when you need to retrieve only some columns of the original entity as part of your query.

When you create a query, most of the time you know the key value and you perform a search using this known value. However, sometimes you need to search using another value or even a subquery.

You can define a search of orders performed by a subquery based on the OrderDetail properties. The following code sample returns the orders related to OrderDetails that contain a product with ProductID equal to 42:
```
from o in context.Orders
where o.OrderDetails.Any(d => d.ProductID == 42)
select o;
```
This code uses the Any method to create a subquery that will return true for the orders where the ProductID of one or more of the OrderDetails entities is equal to 42.

You can also use the Where method to create a nested query. The following code sample returns the orders that have at least one OrderDetail with a UnitPrice greater than 100:
```
from o in context.Orders
where o.OrderDetails.Where(d => d.UnitPrice > 100).Count() > 0
select o;
```
Another way to perform a subquery is to define a query that retrieves the order entities that contain at least one OrderDetail that refers to ProductID equal to 42:
```
from o in context.Orders
from d in o.OrderDetails
where d.ProductID == 42
select o;
```
In this case, the query defines two generator expressions and uses a where clause with the condition on the inner generator variable. This query returns a result that is similar to the previous query that uses the Any method.

You can define a query that uses properties of the details to define a filter on the order entities. The following code sample returns the orders where the total unit price for all details is greater than 1000:
```
from o in context.Orders
where o.OrderDetails.Sum(d => (d.UnitPrice * d.Quantity)) > 1000
select o;
```
You can also get the total of the unit price for related OrderDetails, defining a query that uses the Sum method. You can retrieve the total for all the details or a filtered total for the details:
```
var total = (from o in context.Orders
            where o.EmployeeID == 2
            select o.OrderDetails.Sum(d => (d.UnitPrice * d.Quantity))).Sum();
```
In this query, the Select method returns an IQueryable<decimal> that represents the total of the OrderDetails for each order with an EmployeeID equal to 2. The final Sum method calculates the total amount for the order.

## Ordering the Result of a Query

You can define a query that orders the result using one or more properties of the entities. For example, the following code orders the result by TotalDue :
```
var orders = from o in context.Orders
            orderby o.TotalDue descending
            select o;
```
You can also order using related detail properties. For example, the following code orders the orders by the total unit price of their OrderDetails :
```
var orders = from o in context.Orders
            orderby o.OrderDetails.Sum(d => (d.UnitPrice * d.Quantity))
            select o;
```
## Using SQL Functions

You can use SQL functions for database queries. The Entity Framework provides a set of functions, known as canonical functions, compatible with all providers.

The following query sample uses StartsWith, EndsWith, and Contains methods inside a Where clause:
```
from o in context.Orders
where o.CustomerID.StartsWith("C") || o.CustomerID.EndsWith("s") || o.CustomerID.Contains("ust")
select o;
```
This code defines a query with a Where clause that will return the orders whose CustomerID starts with the letter "C" or ends with the letter "s" or contains the text "ust".

There are many supported canonical functions, for a complete list, see Canonical Functions (Entity SQL) and CLR Method to Canonical Function Mapping.

Finally, you discovered how to use canonical functions to perform mathematical and string operations in your queries.
